indian-startups-aeea936cbb.headline: India’s Startup Funding Map: AI, Sustainability & Deeptech Leading the Next Wave
indian-startups-aeea936cbb.fulltext:
India’s startup funding landscape is shifting again. After a cautious phase marked by slower investment and tighter capital flows, Venture Capital (VC) firms are now placing bigger bets on sectors linked to Artificial Intelligence (AI), sustainability, fintech and deep tech.
Recent investment trends signal that investors are moving away from growth-at-all-cost models & focusing more on long-term value creation.
Startups solving real problems in infrastructure, climate, financial inclusion, and enterprise technology are attracting greater attention in 2026.
As quoted in different industry reports & investor statements, AI-led businesses, climate-focused startups & deeptech firms are now among the fastest-growing investment categories in India’s startup ecosystem.
Also Read: User-Guide: How Indian Startups Can Use GPT-X to Build Faster, Spend Less and Compete Globally
Why Venture Capital Funding Priorities Are Changing
The Indian startup market underwent a correction between 2023 and 2024. Funding volumes slowed globally due to inflation concerns, higher interest rates and reduced risk appetite from investors.
That phase forced startups to focus on profitability, sustainable growth and operational efficiency rather than aggressive expansion.
Now, investors are returning with a more selective approach. Instead of backing businesses built mainly on discounts and rapid customer acquisition, investors are looking for startups that solve structural challenges across industries such as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, agriculture, mobility and energy.
This shift is also being influenced by government-led digital infrastructure projects, India’s semiconductor push, data localisation efforts and rising enterprise demand for AI-driven solutions.
Also Read: Maruti Suzuki Taps Five Indian Startups to Build AI Solutions and Advance EV Battery Recycling
AI Startups Become the Biggest Funding Magnet
Artificial Intelligence has emerged as one of the strongest investment themes globally, and India is seeing the same trend.
Indian AI startups working in automation, enterprise software, generative AI, cybersecurity, healthcare diagnostics and customer support tools are attracting fresh investor interest.
The rise of Generative AI platforms after 2024 changed how investors view software businesses. Startups using AI to reduce operational costs, improve productivity or automate workflows are now seen as scalable and commercially viable.
Large Indian enterprises are also increasing AI adoption across sectors including banking, telecom, retail and logistics. This has opened new business opportunities for SaaS startups and enterprise technology firms.
Investors are particularly focusing on AI startups building India-specific language models, voice technologies, AI infrastructure, and data intelligence tools.
Several global VC firms have already increased allocations for AI-first companies operating in India and Southeast Asia.
Why Is AI Funding Growing Fast?
The market is quite volatile, driven by many factors. AI funding has seen a rising trend, citing different reasons:
1. Enterprise demand is rising across verticals
Indian enterprises are no longer treating AI as an experimental line item. It has moved into the core budget, backed by national frameworks like the NITI Aayog economic roadmap & the ₹10,371 crore IndiaAI Mission.
- Banks use AI for fraud detection and credit underwriting
- Telecom operators use AI for network optimisation and churn prediction
- Retailers automate inventory & demand forecasting
- Logistics firms use it for route planning and warehouse automation.
This scale of usage proves that AI startups are no longer selling a single use case to a single industry. They are now an integral part of the infrastructure that every sector builds on. This materially de-risks the investment thesis for VCs.
2. The cost of building & deploying AI has crashed
Cloud computing has become cheaper and more accessible. Open-source foundation models have matured to the point where they rival proprietary alternatives on many tasks and pre-built APIs mean startups no longer need to train models from scratch.
This has shortened the time-to-market for AI products from years to months. This means lower capital requirements & execution risk, which are the favourite factors investors weigh when writing early-stage cheques.
3. India’s developer and technical talent pool is a structural advantage
India produces one of the largest pools of engineering and computer science graduates in the world. A growing share of that talent is now trained specifically in machine learning, data science and applied AI. This gives Indian AI startups a cost-efficient, high-quality talent advantage over many Western counterparts, allowing them to build faster and scale AI teams more affordably, a point that global investors are increasingly factoring into valuation models.
4. India-specific data & language advantages create defensibility
Global large language models are often weak on Indian languages, dialects, accents & cultural context. Startups focusing on India-first voice AI, vernacular language models & localisation layers are building defensible niches that global players cannot easily compete. Investors view this “local data moat” as a genuine competitive barrier rather than merely a feature.
5. Government policy is actively de-risking the sector
Initiatives around AI infrastructure, data localisation, IndiaAI Mission-style compute, startup support programmes & semiconductor manufacturing incentives are lowering structural barriers for AI companies. Policy reforms reduce long-term uncertainty and make VCs more comfortable committing larger, longer-duration investments.
6. Enterprise SaaS is being re-rated through an AI lens
Traditional SaaS companies that embed AI copilots, automation layers or agentic workflows into their products are commanding stronger valuations than “plain” SaaS peers. This re-rating is pulling capital toward any startup, regardless of original category, that can credibly demonstrate AI-native product architecture, not just an AI feature bolted onto an existing tool.
7. Global capital is actively hunting for the “next market” beyond the US and China
With AI valuations in the US at elevated levels and China facing geopolitical friction with Western capital, global funds are actively scouting India and Southeast Asia as the next large, underpenetrated AI market.
This capital rotation is a meaningful tailwind independent of India’s own domestic fundamentals.
Also Read: A Complete Guide: How to Launch an IPO for Startups in India?
Sustainability and Climate-Tech Startups Gain Investor Attention
Climate-tech and sustainability-focused startups are also becoming major investment targets.
Investors are increasingly backing companies working in electric mobility, battery technology, renewable energy, carbon management, clean manufacturing and waste management.
India’s energy transition goals and net-zero commitments are creating large market opportunities for green technology businesses.
Government initiatives linked to clean energy manufacturing, solar production and electric vehicle expansion are adding momentum to the sector.
Startups working on water conservation, agricultural sustainability and circular economy solutions are also gaining visibility among investors.
What Is Driving Sustainability Investments?
Here’s a collated list of what is driving the funding and investments in sustainability-related projects:
1. ESG is moving from a checkbox to a capital allocation filter
Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) investing is no longer limited to global funds that report to institutional LPs. Domestic Indian family offices and corporate venture arms are also doing so. Growth-stage funds are now building ESG scorecards directly into their diligence process, meaning climate-aligned startups are getting faster access to capital, not just “impact” capital on the margins.
2. Climate risk has become a revenue opportunity, not just a cost centre
The rising frequency of heatwaves, erratic monsoons, water stress, and extreme weather events is forcing the agriculture, insurance, real estate and manufacturing sectors to invest in climate-resilient technologies, from predictive weather analytics to resilient crop and supply chain tools. This has turned climate adaptation from a compliance expense into a genuine, monetisable market.
3. Corporate decarbonisation targets are creating a captive customer base
Large Indian conglomerates and multinationals operating in India have made public net-zero and emissions-reduction commitments. Many lack in-house capability to hit them.
This has created a fast-growing B2B market for carbon accounting, supply chain emissions tracking and clean manufacturing startups, a customer base that climate-tech founders can sell into immediately rather than waiting for consumer adoption curves.
4. Capital-intensive climate hardware is finally getting patient capital
Battery technology, EV components & clean manufacturing demand longer gestation periods & a heavier upfront capital than typical software startups.
A new generation of climate-focused and blended-capital funds, willing to underwrite 7-10 year horizons, has emerged. They specifically fund this category, unlocking a segment that was previously starving of risk capital in India.
Also Read: India’s Startup Funding Slowdown as Venture Capital Turns Cautious Amid Regulatory Concerns
Deeptech Is Moving Beyond Research Labs
Deeptech startups are gradually moving into the mainstream investment ecosystem.
Unlike traditional internet startups, deeptech firms build products around advanced engineering, scientific research and complex technologies.
This includes sectors such as semiconductors, robotics, aerospace, defence technology, quantum computing and advanced manufacturing.
India’s policy push around semiconductor production and electronics manufacturing is helping this category gain momentum.
Several investors now believe India’s next startup wave may come from engineering-led innovation rather than purely consumer-internet businesses.
Why Deeptech Is Becoming Important?
1. Strategic technology independence is now a national priority
Geopolitical tensions and global supply chain disruptions have pushed countries to prioritise domestic capability in chips, AI infrastructure, defence systems and cybersecurity.
This isn’t just policy rhetoric; it translates into direct government procurement, subsidies and long-term contracts that de-risk deeptech business models in ways pure consumer startups never had access to.
2. India’s manufacturing base is expanding rapidly
Production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes across electronics, semiconductors & advanced manufacturing are creating a domestic supply chain. Deeptech startups can potentially join and reduce dependence on imported components. This will also shorten go-to-market timelines for hardware-heavy businesses.
3. Deeptech creates durable, defensible IP
Unlike software businesses, which well-funded competitors can quickly replicate, deeptech companies are built on patents, proprietary engineering, and years of R&D.
They create far higher barriers to entry. Investors backing this category are increasingly willing to accept longer investment horizons in exchange for the stronger moats and premium exit valuations that hard-to-replicate technology can command.
Fintech Continues To Remain Strong
Even with tighter regulations, fintech remains one of India’s most funded startup sectors.
Digital lending, insurance technology, wealth management and embedded finance platforms continue to attract capital.
India’s digital public infrastructure, including Unified Payments Interface (UPI), Aadhaar-based verification systems and account aggregators, has strengthened the fintech ecosystem.

india-deep-tech-2a01f06d67.headline: They spy on India from space. Now an Indian startup is ready to expose them
india-deep-tech-2a01f06d67.fulltext:
They spy on India from space. Now an Indian startup is ready to expose them
Digantara is developing MOSAIC, an autonomous system to detect and track objects moving above India. The effort reflects a wider push to build independent space awareness as satellite activity grows.
On a cold night in Ladakh, a small instrument points silently towards the sky.
It does not know in advance which satellite it is looking for. It is not waiting for an operator to tell it where to turn. Instead, it watches a section of the sky, detects whatever moves through it and begins separating satellites from stars and space debris.
Each passing object can become a piece of a much larger puzzle: Who is above India? When will they return? And what could they be watching?
For a country that once had to carefully conceal its preparations from foreign spy satellites during the Pokhran nuclear tests, those questions are becoming increasingly important.
In the years since Pokhran, the world above India has changed dramatically. Space is no longer occupied by a limited number of satellites operated by a handful of countries. Thousands of satellites now circle the Earth, providing communications, navigation, imagery and intelligence. Modern militaries are increasingly dependent on information flowing through space.
In a post-Operation Sindoor security environment, the ability to understand what is happening in orbit could become as important as monitoring activity on land, at sea or in the air.
India has some space surveillance capability through its Netra programme. But a new generation of Indian companies is attempting to build additional capabilities that could give the country a clearer and more independent picture of what is moving above it.
One such effort is MOSAIC, a space surveillance system being developed by Indian startup Digantara.
The larger ambition is not simply to track space debris or avoid satellite collisions. It is about building what experts call Space Situational Awareness, the ability to know what objects are in space, where they are and where they are likely to move next.
FROM HIDING ON THE GROUND TO WATCHING FROM BELOW
The importance of knowing when satellites are overhead is not new to India.
During the preparations for India's nuclear tests at Pokhran, avoiding detection by foreign surveillance satellites was a critical concern. Activities had to be carefully managed to prevent unusual movement or preparations from being observed from space.
"That episode illustrated a fundamental reality of modern security: before you can hide from something, you need to know when it is looking," said Lt Gen (Retd.) AK Bhatt, Director General, Indian Space Association.
That principle is now becoming even more relevant.
Satellites today can support military operations through imagery, communications, navigation and intelligence. A country that knows when a particular satellite is likely to pass over a sensitive location can better understand when that area may be under observation.
“It all begins with knowing,” as the logic behind space situational awareness suggests. If an object has been detected and catalogued, its orbit can be calculated, allowing future passes to be predicted.
This does not mean that a surveillance network can reveal everything about another country's intentions. But it can help create a picture of the environment in which military and strategic infrastructure operates.
If a particular satellite repeatedly observes a region, that pattern itself may provide useful information. It can indicate increased interest in a location and allow planners to better assess the surveillance environment.
In a future conflict, the challenge may not come from a satellite alone. Space-based systems could provide the communications, navigation, imagery or intelligence needed to support operations on the ground, in the air or at sea.
A coordinated airborne or space-enabled attack would therefore not exist in isolation. Satellites could potentially form part of the larger information network supporting it.
The ability to maintain a continuous picture of objects in orbit could give India an additional layer of awareness around its critical infrastructure and strategic assets.
A SCANNER FOR THE SKY
Traditional space surveillance systems often work like a telescope with an appointment book.
An operator identifies the object they want to observe, calculates where it is expected to be and then directs the instrument towards it.
MOSAIC is designed differently.
According to Anirudh Sharma, Founder and CEO of Digantara, the system functions as a wide-field, autonomous surveillance platform. Once it is switched on and pointed towards a particular portion of the sky, it watches that area and automatically detects and tags everything passing through its field of view.
The system does not need to be told in advance which satellite to track.
Instead, it scans.
Artificial intelligence and machine learning are used to distinguish between stars, satellites and space debris. The processing happens within the system itself, reducing the need for constant human intervention.
Each unit can typically collect data on around 400 to 500 unique objects during a night. An array of such systems, watching different sections of the sky, could collectively build observations of thousands of objects.
The current design uses two cameras, or nodes. Rather than relying on a single 360-degree rotating system, multiple units can be deployed and oriented towards different regions of the sky to increase coverage.
That is important because the challenge is not simply detecting an object once.
Satellites move. Their positions change continuously. Tracking them intermittently can lead to uncertainty about where they are likely to be. Repeated observations can help update their movement and maintain what the space surveillance community calls “custody” of an object.
WHY INDIA CANNOT LOOK UP ALONE
The sky above India cannot be monitored from India alone.
A satellite passing over Ladakh may have been over Australia, Africa or the Pacific hours earlier. To understand its movement accurately, observations from different geographical locations become valuable.
Digantara's network is being deployed across multiple locations, including India, Namibia, Chile and New Mexico, with another deployment planned in Hawaii. Locations are selected largely for clear skies and low light pollution.
The company is also working on space-based sensors, while its ground network is intended to grow over time.
This global approach highlights an important point: space situational awareness cannot realistically be a completely isolated national capability.
India needs sovereign capability, but it will also need cooperation.
Historically, much of the world's space surveillance data has been generated by the extensive sensor network of the United States. Such data has been available to other countries to varying degrees, but dependence on an external source comes with obvious limitations.
A foreign country ultimately decides what information it shares, particularly when sensitive military or strategic assets are involved.
An indigenous capability changes that equation.
It gives India its own observations, its own data and, importantly, something of value to contribute to partnerships with other countries.
The most effective future model may therefore be a combination of Indian-owned systems, commercial innovation and data-sharing with like-minded partners.
MORE THAN SPACE DEBRIS
There is also a civilian side to this technology.
The rapid growth of satellites has created an increasingly crowded orbital environment. Tracking objects is essential for preventing collisions and protecting satellites that provide communications, weather forecasts, navigation and other services.
MOSAIC has also been designed to operate autonomously. It has solar power, onboard computing and communications capability, allowing it to function without continuous human intervention and upload observations within minutes.
Another feature, called “Lost in Space”, allows the system to use patterns of stars to determine its own position without manually entering geographical coordinates. The underlying technology could also have future applications in celestial navigation when GPS is unavailable, denied or spoofed.
The company is additionally exploring a laser-dazzling capability that could temporarily interfere with the optical system of an imaging satellite observing a sensitive location.
Digantara describes the concept as a potential “soft kill” rather than a system intended to physically destroy a satellite. Rapid prototyping is underway, according to the company.
INDIA'S NEW FRONTIER OF AWARENESS
The real significance of MOSAIC may lie in a simple shift in thinking.
For decades, the question was often whether India could launch satellites into space.
Today, the question is also whether India knows what everyone else's satellites are doing.
In the era after Operation Sindoor, India's security calculations increasingly extend across land, sea, air, cyber networks and now space. Critical infrastructure on the ground may be supported, observed or targeted through information flowing from hundreds of kilometres above Earth.
A surveillance network will not eliminate those threats. Nor can India realistically become completely independent of global space data.
But the ability to independently observe, track and predict what is happening overhead could reduce dependence and increase awareness.
From Pokhran, where secrecy demanded knowing when foreign satellites might be watching, to a future in which thousands of objects will cross the sky every night, India's relationship with space has changed.
The country is no longer simply trying to reach orbit.
Increasingly, it is trying to understand and watch the crowded and contested world already there.

global-economics-3fb3f23fc8.headline: ‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade war
global-economics-3fb3f23fc8.fulltext:
Donald Trump has hit back at Canada after a breakdown in negotiations plunged the two countries into a trade war.
In his first public comments since negotiations collapsed on Friday in Washington, the US president wrote on social media: “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!”
“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” he added. “No more!!!”
His comments came after the US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.6bn) worth of Canadian goods, while Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, has vowed to match them “dollar for dollar”.
The US tariffs came into force on Saturday, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Trade experts have predicted that the tariffs could result in some job losses, but the biggest impact is expected to be political, triggering fresh tension between the neighbours.
Both sides blamed the other for the breakdown in talks on Friday. Carney told Canadian journalists that the country was “at war” over trade with the US, after Trump “miscalculated” by escalating his tariff attack.
“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” the Canadian prime minister told reporters in Ottawa. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.”
Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, has said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliatory measures by Canada. He told Fox & Friends Weekend: “We’ve said enough and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains.”
Dan Kelly, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, estimated that 40% of small Canadian exporters will be directly hit by the US tariffs, and that nearly one-third expect their revenues will drop by 50% or more as a result.
The escalation was also met with anger by Democrat lawmakers and governors from US states that border Canada including Minnesota, New York and Washington.
New York governor Kathy Hochul posted on X: “Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That’s Trump’s economic policy in a nutshell.”
Minnesota senator Amy Klobuchar, said the new tariffs meant “higher costs for small businesses, farmers, and all Minnesota families.”
She wrote on X: “Canada is Minnesota’s #1 trading partner. Minnesotans are paying for Trump’s chaos.”
Carney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England, was elected as Canada’s prime minister last year after campaigning to lead a fightback against Trump, who has suggested he wants to make Canada a 51st state with “economic force”.
Carney’s “dollar for dollar” tariffs are expected to take effect from 8 September, with new levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The escalation has also called into question the future of the North American trade pact between the US, Canada and Mexico, known as USMCA.
The pact, which was signed by Trump during his first term, governs about $2tn annually in goods and services between the three countries. Trump refused to renew the USMCA this summer after Canada and Mexico formally requested for it to be renewed for another 16 years.
When asked how the US-Canadian collapse in trade talks would affect the USMCA, Carney said it was “certainly not good news”.
Increasingly aggressive rhetoric and trade policy from the Trump administration has damaged US-Canadian relations, with tourism also suffering – there was a 21% drop in Canadians entering New York state in 2025 and 3mn fewer visits compared with the previous year.
Furthermore, a petition to expel the US ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, from the country has gathered around 248,000 signatures since late July, according to the Associated Press.
This year a poll by Globe and Mail newspaper found that only 9% of Canadians agreed that the US was a “trustworthy ally”, and that 51% of those polled had cancelled American trips in reaction to comments by Trump.

Sneha Ganguly, researcher, the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre
They found the heavy rainfall observed in 2026 wasn’t exceptional, recurring every one to two years.
The team also found no clear link to human-induced rise in global temperatures.
“When we combine the observational results with the climate models, we again found no detectable climate change signal in either type of events,” co-author Mariam Zachariah, from Imperial College London, said at the briefing.
Instead, the study found the main drivers of this year’s catastrophic floods were land-use changes, sedimentation, and structural vulnerability.
The Brahmaputra River itself carries large amounts of sediments every monsoon that raises its riverbed, reducing channel capacity, meaning water flows out. This season’s flooding was, however, worsened by unplanned urbanisation and deforestation that has degraded wetlands and disrupted natural drainage.
Sneha Ganguly, study co-author from the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, said at the briefing that evidence from a review of 35 studies suggested “unplanned urbanisation, deforestation, poor drainage, inadequate structural flood management measures, and other anthropogenic changes now outweigh natural rainfall variability in explaining flood frequency.”
The report also highlights historical roots of vulnerability: Colonial land appropriation for tea plantations forced Indigenous communities onto marginal, highly flood-prone riverbanks and sandbars (char areas), creating systemic patterns of exposure that persist today.
While Assam has built extensive concrete embankments, the report warns that heavy reliance on rigid infrastructure can actually worsen flooding by trapping silt and increasing the risk of breaches.
“Future adaptation will therefore need to focus less on controlling rivers and maybe more on working with them to combine targeted engineering with floodplain restoration, wetland conservation, reducing development in floodplains, improved drainage, and community preparedness,” Ganguly said.

  August 23, 2026 / 09:14 IST  
         The US-India trade agreement is “almost” finalised in principle, with legal and technical language being worked out before the deal is concluded, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said on Saturday.
Speaking at The Economic Times World Leaders Forum, Gor said the remaining work largely involved reconfiguring parts of the agreement's text.
“The trade deal is, in principle, almost everything is done,” he said, adding that the time taken to finalise it was due to the legal and technical language that still needed to be sorted out.
Gor also sought to draw a distinction between a bipartisan push in the US Congress for tariffs on countries purchasing Russian oil and the position of the Donald Trump administration.
The proposed legislation, which could impose 100% tariffs on countries buying Russian oil, was being “pushed by the Congress in a very bipartisan way”, he said.
“This is not something that you have seen the White House advocate. You won't find a clip of President Trump pushing it,” Gor said.
While acknowledging that the proposed bill could affect India, Gor said Trump had been focused on bringing the Russia-Ukraine war to an end.
“President from day one has been wanting to end this war between Russia and Ukraine, and he's determined,” he said, adding that it was “vitally important” for the conflict to end.
Trump has ‘tremendous respect’ for Modi
Gor said Trump and Prime Minister Narendra Modi share a “deep and personal friendship”, describing both leaders as results-driven and action-oriented.
“They are both forward leaning, and they want action fast, and they’re results-driven. Our President has tremendous respect for the Prime Minister,” he said.
Gor said Trump particularly remembered Modi's support during the period when he was out of office following the 2020 US presidential election.
“When you're up, when you're in the Oval Office, everybody wants to be your friend. But when you're out, that's when you can really realise who your friends are. And Prime Minister Narendra Modi was a true friend to him at that time,” Gor said. He added that the relationship between the two leaders was strengthened by mutual trust.
Highlighting India's strategic importance to Washington, Gor pointed to the visits of senior US administration officials “India matters to us, and we want to have the highest individuals from our government being here and participating,” he said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had spent five days in India in May and is scheduled to return for another multi-day visit in October, Gor said.
“That's unheard of for us,” he added.
Gor said the US-India relationship would play a defining role on the global stage.
On the US-China relationship and Washington's ties with countries that have close relations with Pakistan, Gor said the US maintained bilateral relationships across the world.
“You can't pick who your neighbours are,” he said. “Whether we like it or not, we have to work with the governments that are there.”

Zelensky details rift with Ukraine’s dismissed defence minister Fedorov
The president said inaccurate defence ministry information contributed to an awkward encounter with Trump over the use of Starlink in Russia
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believes actions taken by dismissed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, including his involvement in mass protests and calls for an election, were misguided, as he publicly detailed their dispute for the first time.
Zelensky also alluded to problematic decisions over defence spending and said inaccurate information provided by the Defence Ministry contributed to an awkward encounter with US President Donald Trump over the use of Starlink in Russia.
Zelensky disclosed figures showing Ukraine’s growing shortage of Patriot air-defence missiles needed to counter Russian ballistic attacks, with deliveries from Western allies declining in the past three years even as Russian missile strikes intensified.
He highlighted battlefield gains, however, saying Ukrainian forces have almost completely recaptured the Dnipropetrovsk region, with only about 10 sq km (around 4 square miles) remaining under Russian control.
The Ukrainian president made the remarks during a two-hour off-the-record meeting with reporters on Saturday, with a transcript released publicly on Sunday.
Zelensky’s first public comments on Fedorov dismissal
His comments ranged widely, covering the latest battlefield developments, efforts to counter Russian ballistic attacks, the state of peace negotiations, Ukraine’s budgetary challenges and the political turmoil surrounding Fedorov’s dismissal.

other-interests-8423c2ea1a.headline: Patricio Segura, journalist who defended Patagonia’s rivers, died of hantavirus, aged 54
other-interests-8423c2ea1a.fulltext:
The fight to stop five dams on the Baker and Pascua rivers began in one of Chile’s least populous regions, far from Santiago, where national energy policy was set. HidroAysén said Chile needed the project to meet rising demand for electricity. Patricio Segura, working from Aysén in Chilean Patagonia, spent years picking apart that case. He read the filings, explained what the reservoirs and transmission lines would mean on the ground, and helped residents prepare their own arguments. The dams were never built.
There was an obvious complication: Segura was also one of the organizers. Through the Corporación Privada para el Desarrollo de Aysén, or CODESA, he helped organize local opposition and worked on communications for Patagonia Sin Represas. International groups eventually joined, helping make the Baker and Pascua global symbols of river defense. Segura welcomed the wider audience but repeatedly insisted that decisions stay with the people who lived in Aysén.
Born in Iquique, he studied journalism at the Universidad Católica del Norte and arrived in Coyhaique in 1995. He wrote about science, tourism, corruption, and politics. His reporting appeared in local outlets and national publications, and for 15 years he contributed investigations and columns to Patagon Journal.
HidroAysén’s defeat left plenty else for him to cover. Salmon companies were spreading through the Patagonian fjords, leaving pollution and damaged seabeds while gaining political clout. Mines closed or changed hands without adequately addressing contaminated sites. Rural estates were divided into hundreds of speculative plots, or megaloteos, creating settlements outside normal planning and the provision of public services. Segura examined the permits and court cases, checked company claims, and named the officials responsible.
Conservation groups did not escape his scrutiny. Segura objected when wealthy outsiders acquired land or promoted protected areas without giving local communities a meaningful role. In a three-part series, he described private conservation, tourism, and rural subdivision as “green Monopoly.” Protecting Patagonia, he argued, did not give philanthropists the right to decide its future. “What cannot happen,” he once said, “is for outsiders to dictate how things should be.” He believed conservation imposed from elsewhere could reproduce the inequalities of industrial development, and said so even when it meant criticizing his own movement.
Segura did not mind giving offense, but he did his homework. In a column on salmon farming, a comparison with Mr. Burns’s control of Springfield in The Simpsons came only after a labor study, a diver’s death, and a Supreme Court ruling. His longer investigations worked the same way, drawing on official minutes, correspondence, company statements, and residents’ testimony. Allies received the same treatment when he thought they were wrong.
Segura died from hantavirus on August 21st, aged 54. Less than a month earlier, Patagon Journal published his last column, “The Other AI: Ancestral Intelligence.” It examined knowledge built over generations of observation by Indigenous peoples, long dismissed as superstition. Segura believed that dismissal had done lasting damage. For him, that history contained “a lesson we need to reclaim.”

beyond-your-beat-a28f6af090.headline: Padikkal tons up again as India dominate Day 1 in Colombo
beyond-your-beat-a28f6af090.fulltext:
Padikkal tons up again as India dominate Day 1 in Colombo
Devdutt Padikkal scored a hundred for the second game in a row to put India in a strong position against Sri Lanka.
India assumed a position of strength at the end of the first day of the second World Test Championship match between India and Sri Lanka at Colombo, thanks to a century by Devdutt Padikkal, who carried his fine form from the previous game in Galle, as the visitors ended the day at 300/5.
India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak was left to rue the loss of Padikkal (117) and Ravindra Jadeja (43) late in the day, but still believes his team is well placed to put together a large total.
"I think all in all, apart from couple of dismissals which you feel we could have avoided, I think we batted really well," Kotak said.
"And all in all, we can't complain on day one. Because in the first session, the ball was moving and there was some moisture. Even I felt that the spinners were getting a turn in the first session. So, I think we betted well."
Dhruv Jurel (7*) and debutant Saransh Jain (4*) are the not out players for India at stumps, while Kotak revealed Rishabah Pant would be fit to bat on the second day after the left-hander was forced to retire hurt early in his innings on Sunday.
Sri Lanka bowling coach Ryan van Niekerk remained optimistic at stumps, believing his side was still well in the contest should they be able to pick up early wickets on the second day.
"We've still got a new ball in the morning to use and hopefully a fairly fresh Asitha (Fernando) and Lahiru (Kumara) to start the day," van Niekerk said.
"So if we can make some early inroads, that would be fantastic for us."
Opting to bat first after winning the toss at the Sinhalese Sports Club (SSC) ground, India faced immediate challenges against a disciplined Sri Lankan pace attack.
Yashasvi Jaiswal and KL Rahul safely navigated the initial overs, adding 37 runs for the opening stand. Lahiru Kumara removed Rahul for 18, safely caught behind by Niroshan Dickwella to deal India the first blow of the morning.
Jaiswal looked aggressive and confident at the other end, striking nine boundaries in a brisk 45 before an excellent delivery from Asitha Fernando shattered his stumps.
Captain Shubman Gill and Padikkal then orchestrated a brilliant recovery, keeping the hosts at bay with a watchful yet decisive 120-run partnership for the third wicket.
Showing immense patience, the duo weathered probing spells from the pacers and the left-arm spin of Prabath Jayasuriya. Gill, leading by example, brought up a composed half-century in 108 balls, anchoring the innings with a blend of solid defence and calculated aggression. His resilient knock was eventually ended by Fernando, caught behind on the stroke of Tea for 50.
Unfazed by the loss of his skipper, Padikkal blossomed in the final session, transitioning smoothly from accumulator to enforcer. He drove and pulled his way to a magnificent 117 off 193 deliveries, an innings beautifully studded with 12 boundaries. His masterful century completely frustrated the Sri Lankan bowling unit and laid a formidable foundation for the visitors.
India suffered a blow when Pant was forced to retire hurt after adding just three runs on the board after a short ball hit his wrists. That brought the veteran Ravindra Jadeja to the crease, who showcased all his experience at a crucial juncture for India.
Jadeja provided excellent support down the order, contributing a crucial 43 off 83 balls.
Keshara Nuwantha claimed the prized wicket of Padikkal, castling the centurion to secure his maiden Test wicket, while Fernando returned after Sri Lanka took the new ball to claim his third scalp of the day by dismissing Jadeja.
At stumps, Jurel (7*) and Jain (4*) remained unbeaten, guiding India to a strong 300/5 in 85 overs. For Sri Lanka, Fernando was the undisputed standout performer with impressive figures of 3/46 in his 16 overs.
As Day 2 approaches, India will look to maximise their commanding first-innings total, while the hosts will desperately seek early morning breakthroughs to wrest the initiative back in their favour.

ERA Research Manager Opportunities 2026: AI Safety, Governance & Biosecurity Roles in Cambridge and Remote – Apply By 28 August 2026
The Existential Risk Alliance (ERA) is inviting applications for four Research Manager positions supporting its internationally recognised programmes in frontier AI safety, AI governance, AI security, and biosecurity. Based in Cambridge, United Kingdom, with both full-time and part-time opportunities available, the roles offer experienced researchers and research leaders the chance to shape one of the world’s largest AI safety talent development programmes.
ERA welcomes applications from exceptional candidates across the globe and offers visa sponsorship and relocation support for eligible international applicants. The application deadline for all positions is 28 August 2026.
About ERA
ERA is a Cambridge-based talent and research organisation dedicated to reducing catastrophic risks arising from frontier artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. Since its establishment, the organisation has supported more than 200 researchers from over 30 countries, helping develop careers in AI safety, governance, biosecurity, and public policy.
Its fellows receive mentorship from leading organisations including the UK AI Security Institute (AISI), RAND, Governance of AI (GovAI), and Google DeepMind. ERA also hosts high-profile initiatives such as the Technical AI Governance Forum, the Vegas AI Security Forum, the ERA:AI Fellowship, the AIxBiosecurity Fellowship, and the Frontier AI Security Residency.
As ERA expands in 2027, Research Managers will play a central role in building research infrastructure, supporting emerging scholars, and developing strategic initiatives that strengthen global AI safety and biosecurity.
Available Positions
ERA is currently recruiting for four positions:
- ERA:AI Research Manager (Full-time) – Cambridge, UK
- ERA:AI Research Manager (Part-time) – Remote or Cambridge
- AIxBio Research Manager (Full-time) – Cambridge, UK
- AIxBio Research Manager (Part-time) – Remote or Cambridge
Full-time positions offer salaries ranging from £60,000–£90,000, while part-time roles are paid on a pro-rated basis with flexibility for exceptional candidates. The preferred start date is 1 November 2026, although earlier starts may be possible.
What Research Managers Do
Research Managers provide the intellectual foundation of ERA’s programmes. Rather than serving purely administrative functions, they guide ambitious research, mentor early-career fellows, identify neglected research questions, and help translate complex ideas into rigorous, policy-relevant projects.
Successful candidates will oversee portfolios of research projects while working closely with fellows, mentors, policymakers, technical researchers, and institutional partners. They will also contribute to ERA’s long-term strategy by identifying emerging priorities in AI safety, governance, verification, security, and biosecurity.
The role combines research leadership, programme design, mentorship, community building, and strategic thinking within one of the fastest-evolving fields in technology governance.
Eligibility and Candidate Profile
ERA is interested in diverse candidate profiles and does not expect applicants to satisfy every listed criterion. Strong candidates are likely to demonstrate substantial expertise in either AI safety and governance or biosecurity, together with excellent research judgement and experience evaluating or conducting high-quality research.
Applicants should possess outstanding written and verbal communication skills, strong organisational abilities, and the capacity to work independently within highly collaborative environments.
For ERA:AI roles, experience in frontier AI, governance, alignment, control, verification, or technical AI policy is particularly valuable. For AIxBio roles, expertise in biosecurity, public health, biological risk, or related research areas is especially relevant.
Experience mentoring researchers, reviewing research proposals, managing research portfolios, or building collaborations across academia and policy institutions is considered highly advantageous.
Benefits and International Support
ERA offers an attractive benefits package designed to support both professional development and employee wellbeing. Benefits include:
- Competitive salary based on experience
- £5,000 annual professional development budget
- Productivity and equipment allowance
- 10% employer pension contribution
- Private health insurance, including dental and vision
- Four weeks of recommended paid time off
- Visa sponsorship for eligible international applicants
- Relocation support for successful overseas candidates
These benefits are complemented by a mission-driven workplace that emphasises intellectual autonomy, collaboration, and meaningful societal impact.
Application Process
The recruitment process has been designed to identify exceptional research talent while respecting candidates’ time through compensated assessment stages.
The process includes:
- Initial application with a CV or LinkedIn profile and brief motivation questions.
- Interview with the ERA team.
- Paid work trial for full-time applicants.
- Reference checks followed by final offers, expected around late September 2026.
Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis, making early submission highly advantageous.
How to Strengthen an Application
Applicants should present a CV that clearly demonstrates research achievements, publications, mentorship experience, project leadership, and collaborations with academic or policy institutions. Rather than listing responsibilities, candidates should emphasise measurable research impact, influential publications, grants, fellowships, and interdisciplinary work.
The motivation statement should explain why the applicant is committed to mitigating catastrophic risks from frontier AI or biosecurity and demonstrate familiarity with the evolving research landscape. Strong applications also show an ability to identify important research questions, evaluate evidence critically, and translate technical work into decision-relevant policy outcomes.
Candidates with experience connecting academia, government, and industry should highlight examples of successful collaboration, as these relationships are central to ERA’s research model.
Why This Opportunity Matters
The ERA Research Manager positions offer a rare opportunity to shape the future of frontier AI safety and biosecurity while mentoring the next generation of researchers. With substantial autonomy, international collaboration, and direct engagement with leading organisations in AI governance, the roles provide an exceptional platform for scholars seeking to combine rigorous research with real-world policy impact.
